sacVsPrice.title: SAC vs Price: which amortization system to choose?
sacVsPrice.description: Understand the differences between SAC and Price systems and discover which is better for your mortgage.
sacVsPrice.metaTitle: SAC vs Price: which amortization system to choose?
sacVsPrice.metaDescription: Understand the differences between SAC and Price, compare payments and total interest, and discover which amortization system is better for your mortgage.

content.intro: When you take out a mortgage, you need to choose between two amortization systems: SAC (Constant Amortization System) or Price (Price Table). This choice directly impacts your payment amounts and total interest paid.

whatIsSac.title: What is the SAC System?
whatIsSac.p1: In the SAC system, the amortization (the part of the payment that reduces the debt) is constant throughout the loan. This means you pay the same amortization amount every month.
whatIsSac.p2: Since interest is calculated on the outstanding balance, which decreases each month, payments start higher and decrease over time.

whatIsPrice.title: What is the Price Table?
whatIsPrice.p1: In the Price Table, payments are fixed throughout the loan. This makes financial planning easier since you know exactly how much you'll pay each month.
whatIsPrice.p2: However, at the beginning, most of the payment is interest. The amortization increases gradually over time.

comparison.title: Practical comparison
comparison.intro: See an example with a $300,000 loan over 360 months (30 years) at 10% per year:

sacBetter.title: Choose SAC if:
items: You can afford higher payments at the beginning
You want to pay less interest overall
Your income tends to decrease in the future (retirement)

priceBetter.title: Choose Price if:
items: You need smaller, fixed payments
You value budget predictability
Your income tends to increase over time

tip.title: Important tip
tip.text: Use our mortgage calculator to simulate both scenarios with your actual numbers and compare side by side.

q1.question: Which system has lower payments at the beginning?
q1.answer: The Price Table has lower payments at the beginning. In SAC, the first payments are higher but decrease over time.

q2.question: In which system do I pay less interest overall?
q2.answer: In the SAC system you pay less total interest because you amortize the balance faster. The difference can reach 30-40% depending on the term and rate.

q3.question: Can I switch from SAC to Price during the loan?
q3.answer: Generally no. The system is defined in the contract. Some institutions allow portability where you can renegotiate terms, but it's not guaranteed.

q4.question: Which is more common in Brazil?
q4.answer: SAC is more common in Brazilian mortgages, especially those from the Housing Finance System (SFH). The Price Table is more used for car financing and personal loans.

q5.question: Does extra amortization work the same in both systems?
q5.answer: Yes, you can make extra amortizations in both systems. The difference is that in SAC the effect is more immediate on the next payments, while in Price the impact is more distributed.

jurosCompostos.title: Compound interest: what it is and how to calculate
jurosCompostos.description: Understand the power of compound interest and learn to calculate your money's growth over time.
jurosCompostos.metaTitle: Compound Interest: what it is and how to calculate
jurosCompostos.metaDescription: Learn what compound interest is, how it works and how to calculate it. Discover the power of interest on interest for your investments.

content.intro: Compound interest is known as "interest on interest". Unlike simple interest, where the return is calculated only on the initial amount, in compound interest the return is calculated on the accumulated value.

formula.title: The compound interest formula
formula.text: A = P × (1 + r)^t, where A is the final amount, P is the principal, r is the interest rate and t is the time.

example.title: Practical example
example.text: If you invest $10,000 at 1% per month for 12 months:

power.title: The power of time
power.text: The longer the term, the greater the difference between simple and compound interest. In 10 years, $10,000 at 1% per month becomes $33,003.87 with compound interest, but only $22,000 with simple interest.

tips.title: How to leverage compound interest
items: Start investing as early as possible
Reinvest the returns
Maintain consistency in contributions
Avoid unnecessary withdrawals

q1.question: What's the difference between simple and compound interest?
q1.answer: In simple interest, the return is always calculated on the initial value. In compound interest, the return is calculated on the accumulated value (initial + previous interest), creating the "interest on interest" effect.

q2.question: How to calculate compound interest in a calculator?
q2.answer: Use the formula A = P × (1 + r)^t or our compound interest calculator. Just enter the initial value, interest rate and period to see the result.

q3.question: Does compound interest work against me in debts?
q3.answer: Yes! Just as it makes your investment grow, compound interest makes your debts grow quickly. That's why you should pay off high-interest debts as quickly as possible.

q4.question: What's the best compounding frequency?
q4.answer: The more frequent the compounding, the better for investments (daily > monthly > annual). For the same nominal rate, daily interest yields more than monthly over the year.

q5.question: How to convert monthly rate to annual?
q5.answer: Use the formula: Annual rate = (1 + monthly rate)^12 - 1. For example, 1% per month equals 12.68% per year, not 12%.

tir.title: IRR: what is Internal Rate of Return and how to calculate
tir.description: Learn what IRR is, how to interpret it and when to use it to evaluate investments.
tir.metaTitle: IRR: what is Internal Rate of Return
tir.metaDescription: Understand what IRR (Internal Rate of Return) is, how to calculate and interpret it. Learn to use IRR to compare investments.

content.intro: IRR (Internal Rate of Return) is the discount rate that makes the NPV (Net Present Value) of a cash flow equal to zero. In other words, it's the implicit return of an investment.

howItWorks.title: How does IRR work?
howItWorks.text: IRR considers all cash flows of an investment (inflows and outflows) and calculates what the annualized rate of return would be. It's especially useful for comparing investments with different cash flow patterns.

interpretation.title: How to interpret IRR?
items: IRR > hurdle rate: viable investment
IRR < hurdle rate: investment not recommended
The higher the IRR, the better the investment return

example.title: Practical example
example.text: You invest $10,000 and receive $3,000 per year for 5 years. The IRR of this investment is approximately 15.24% per year.

limitations.title: IRR Limitations
items: Assumes reinvestments are made at the same rate
May have multiple solutions with non-conventional flows
Doesn't consider the absolute size of the investment

q1.question: What's the difference between IRR and ROI?
q1.answer: ROI shows the total percentage return without considering time. IRR shows the annualized rate of return, considering when each cash flow occurs.

q2.question: Does IRR work for any investment?
q2.answer: IRR works best for investments with conventional cash flows (negative initial investment followed by positive returns). Alternating flows may generate multiple IRRs.

q3.question: How to calculate IRR manually?
q3.answer: Manual calculation is iterative and laborious. Use our IRR calculator or functions like IRR() in Excel/Google Sheets to get the result quickly.

q4.question: Does negative IRR mean I lost money?
q4.answer: A negative IRR indicates that the present value of outflows is greater than inflows, meaning you're losing money on this investment.

q5.question: Should I use IRR or NPV to decide?
q5.answer: Use both! IRR is good for comparing returns, but NPV shows the absolute value generated. For mutually exclusive projects, prefer NPV.

rendaFixa.title: Fixed Income: CDI, IPCA+ and Selic — which to choose?
rendaFixa.description: Compare the main types of fixed income and understand when to use each one.
rendaFixa.metaTitle: Fixed Income: CDI, IPCA+ and Selic
rendaFixa.metaDescription: Compare fixed income investments: CDB, Treasury Selic, IPCA+. Understand the differences and discover which is best for your profile.

content.intro: Fixed income is a category of investments where you know (or can estimate) how much you'll receive at maturity. The main indexes are CDI, IPCA and Selic.

prefixado.title: Fixed Rate
prefixado.text: Rate defined at the time of application. You know exactly how much you'll receive at maturity. Good when expecting falling interest rates.

cdi.title: Floating Rate (CDI)
cdi.text: Return linked to CDI, which follows Selic. Ideal for emergency fund and short terms, as it follows interest rate variations.

ipca.title: IPCA+
ipca.text: Return = IPCA (inflation) + fixed rate. Protects your purchasing power and guarantees real gain. Ideal for long-term goals.

comparison.title: When to use each type?
items: Emergency fund: Treasury Selic or CDB with daily liquidity
Short term (up to 2 years): Floating rate (CDI)
Medium term (2-5 years): Fixed rate or IPCA+
Long term (5+ years): IPCA+

taxes.title: Taxation
taxes.text: Most fixed income investments follow the regressive income tax table: 22.5% up to 180 days, 20% from 181 to 360 days, 17.5% from 361 to 720 days, 15% above 720 days.

q1.question: Is CDB better than Treasury bonds?
q1.answer: It depends. CDBs may offer better rates but have bank credit risk. Treasury bonds are government-guaranteed. For amounts up to R$250k, CDBs have FGC guarantee.

q2.question: What does 100% of CDI mean?
q2.answer: It means the investment yields exactly the same as the CDI rate. 110% of CDI means it yields 10% more than CDI, and 90% of CDI means 10% less.

q3.question: Can IPCA+ have negative returns?
q3.answer: At maturity, no — you always receive IPCA + contracted rate. But if you sell before maturity, the value may fluctuate downward (mark-to-market).

q4.question: What's the difference between CDI and Selic?
q4.answer: They're very close. Selic is the basic interest rate set by the Central Bank. CDI is the interbank lending rate, which closely follows Selic (usually 0.1% below).

q5.question: Are LCI and LCA better for being tax-exempt?
q5.answer: Not always. Compare the net rate. A CDB at 110% of CDI with tax may yield more than an LCI at 90% of CDI without tax, depending on the term.

financiamentoVsConsorcio.title: Mortgage vs Consortium: which to choose?
financiamentoVsConsorcio.description: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of mortgages and consortiums to decide which is better for you.
financiamentoVsConsorcio.metaTitle: Mortgage vs Consortium: which to choose?
financiamentoVsConsorcio.metaDescription: Compare mortgage and consortium: interest, payments, terms and when to use each. Discover which is better for buying your home or car.

content.intro: Mortgages and consortiums are ways to acquire high-value goods, but they work very differently. Understanding these differences is essential to make the best choice.

financiamento.title: How mortgages work
financiamento.text: In a mortgage, you receive the money immediately and pay installments with interest over time. It's ideal for those who need the asset now.

consorcio.title: How consortiums work
consorcio.text: In a consortium, you participate in a group and are contemplated by lottery or bid. There's no interest, but there's an administration fee.
cons: Don't know when you'll be contemplated

whenToUse.title: When to use each one?
whenToUse.financiamento: Use mortgage if you need the asset now (already have paid housing) and have down payment available.
whenToUse.consorcio: Use consortium if you can wait, have no urgency and want to pay less overall.

q1.question: Consortium has no interest, but is it cheaper?
q1.answer: Generally yes. Even with administration fee and annual adjustment, the total cost of consortium is usually 15-30% less than mortgage.

q2.question: Can I be contemplated in the first month?
q2.answer: Yes, by lottery. But don't count on it for planning. The average contemplation by lottery is between 30-50% of the total term.

q3.question: What is a bid in consortium?
q3.answer: A bid is an offer to advance payments to be contemplated faster. Whoever offers the highest bid (in % of credit) is contemplated. You can use FGTS as bid in real estate consortiums.

q4.question: Can I quit the consortium?
q4.answer: Yes, but you only receive the money back when the group ends or when you're drawn as a quitter. There are also administrative discounts.

q5.question: Is mortgage better if Selic falls?
q5.answer: If you contract with a fixed rate, it doesn't change. With floating rate (TR), there may be reduction. But consortium also becomes more attractive with low Selic (lower opportunity cost).

basics.title: What is a mortgage loan and how do interest and principal work?
basics.p1: In a mortgage-style loan, you pay for the property over time in monthly installments. Each installment typically includes interest (the cost of borrowing) and principal (the part that reduces the remaining balance).
basics.p2: As months pass, the remaining balance usually decreases. Because interest is calculated on the remaining balance, the interest portion often falls over time, while the principal portion may be constant (SAC) or adjusted to keep payments more stable (Price).

sacVsPrice.title: SAC vs Price: what’s the difference?
sacVsPrice.intro: SAC and Price are ways to distribute interest and principal over time. The total interest paid and the payment profile can change significantly.

sac.title: SAC system (constant principal)
sac.body: In SAC, the principal portion is (roughly) constant. Payments typically start higher and decrease over time because interest drops as the remaining balance shrinks.

price.title: Price table (more constant payments)
price.body: In the Price system, the payment tends to be more constant at the beginning. The composition changes: you pay more interest early on and more principal later.

sacVsPrice.tip: Tip: use the simulator to compare total interest and the first/last payment under each system.

amortizationTable.title: How to read the amortization schedule
amortizationTable.intro: The amortization schedule shows, month by month, how the loan evolves. You will typically see columns such as:
amortizationTable.b1: Opening balance: how much you owe at the start of the month.
amortizationTable.b2: Interest: interest paid that month (calculated on the balance).
amortizationTable.b3: Principal: the part of the payment that reduces the balance.
amortizationTable.b4: Payment: what you pay in that month (by system rules).
amortizationTable.b5: Ending balance: how much you still owe after the month’s payment.

extraAmortization.title: Extra payments: reduce term or reduce payment
extraAmortization.intro: Extra payments are additional amounts (on top of the regular payment) that reduce the remaining balance faster. This typically reduces total interest and can shorten the loan.

extraAmortization.note: The exact effect depends on bank rules and your contract. Treat the result as an estimate and confirm the rules with your lender.

q1.question: How do I calculate mortgage payments?
q1.answer: Payments depend on the financed amount (loan amount minus down payment), the interest rate, the term, and the amortization system (SAC or Price). This simulator estimates payments and shows month-by-month details in the amortization schedule.

q2.question: Which is better: SAC or Price?
q2.answer: It depends on your goal. SAC typically starts with higher payments that decrease over time; Price tends to be more constant. Compare total interest, the first/last payment, and your cash-flow needs.

q3.question: What is the remaining balance?
q3.answer: The remaining (outstanding) balance is how much you still owe. It decreases as you pay principal. Interest is calculated on the remaining balance, so extra payments can reduce total interest significantly.

q4.question: Are extra payments worth it?
q4.answer: Often yes: paying extra reduces the balance faster, usually lowering total interest and potentially shortening the term. Whether it’s optimal depends on your loan rate and alternative investment returns.

q5.question: Does this simulator include APR/CET, insurance, and bank fees?
q5.answer: Not necessarily. This is an educational estimate focused on interest/principal mechanics. APR/CET, insurance, fees, taxes, and contract-specific rules can materially change real payments and total cost.

q6.question: What interest rate should I use?
q6.answer: Use the annual rate provided by your lender (ideally the effective rate). If you only have a nominal rate or an APR/CET-style figure, simulate multiple scenarios and confirm with the lender what applies to your contract.

q7.question: Can I use this calculator for any type of loan?
q7.answer: It’s best suited for mortgage-style loans that follow SAC/Price amortization logic. Other loans may have different fees, taxes, and amortization methods.

basics.title: What is a consortium and how it works
basics.p1: A consortium is a planned purchase method where a group of people come together to acquire assets (real estate, vehicles, etc.) without needing traditional bank financing. Each participant pays monthly installments that are divided between the common fund (for contemplation) and the administration fee.
basics.p2: Contemplation can happen by lottery or bid. When contemplated, you receive the credit letter to acquire the asset. Installments continue to be paid until the end of the term, but now you already have the asset in hand.
basics.p3: An important advantage of consortiums is that there are no interest rates like in traditional financing. The cost is in the administration fee and, eventually, the premium (if buying a contemplated letter) or bid (to anticipate contemplation).

howItWorks.title: How consortiums work: common fund, administration fee, and contemplation
howItWorks.intro: Consortiums work with three main components:

fundoComum.title: Common Fund
fundoComum.body: Part of the installment that goes to the common fund, used to contemplate participants. When you are contemplated, you receive the accumulated value from the common fund to acquire the asset.

taxaAdmin.title: Administration Fee
taxaAdmin.body: Fee charged by the consortium administrator to manage the group. It's calculated on the total asset value and distributed throughout the installments. There are no interest rates as in financing, but this fee represents the cost of the consortium. Typical values range between 12% and 20% of the asset value.

contemplacao.title: Contemplation
contemplacao.body: The moment when you receive the credit letter to acquire the asset. It can happen by lottery (monthly) or by bid (when you offer an extra amount to be contemplated earlier). After contemplation, you continue paying installments, but you can already use the asset.

bidPremium.title: Bid and Premium: differences and when to use
bidPremium.intro: Bid and premium are two ways to anticipate or facilitate contemplation in a consortium:

lance.title: Bid
lance.body: Extra amount you pay to be contemplated before the lottery. The bid reduces the consortium term, as you pay additional installments in advance. It's a strategy for those who need the asset faster.

agio.title: Premium
agio.body: Amount paid to buy an already contemplated consortium letter from another participant. When buying a contemplated letter, you receive the asset immediately, but pay an additional amount (premium) beyond the asset value. It's useful when you need the asset quickly and don't want to wait for lottery or give a bid.

correction.title: Annual correction: INCC, IPCA, and installment adjustments
correction.intro: Consortium installments are corrected annually by inflation indices:
correction.c1: INCC (National Construction Cost Index): used for real estate consortiums, reflects construction cost variations
correction.c2: IPCA (Broad National Consumer Price Index): used for other types of consortiums (vehicles, services, etc.)
correction.c3: The correction is applied annually (every 12 months), increasing the value of future installments. That's why extra amortizations can generate savings by avoiding adjustments on larger amounts.

extraAmortization.title: Extra amortization in consortium: reduce term or reduce installment
extraAmortization.intro: Just like in financing, you can make extra amortizations in a consortium to reduce total cost or term:
extraAmortization.prazo: Reduce term: installments remain the same value, but you finish earlier. Ideal when you have extra money and want to pay off faster.
extraAmortization.parcela: Reduce installment: the term remains the same, but future installments become smaller. Useful when you want to ease monthly cash flow.
extraAmortization.note: Extra amortizations in consortiums generate savings because they avoid annual correction (INCC/IPCA) on larger amounts. The more you prepay, the more you save on future adjustments.

q1.question: How do I calculate consortium installments?
q1.answer: Consortium installments are calculated by dividing the asset value by the number of months, plus the administration fee distributed over the term. The base installment is corrected annually by indices like INCC (real estate) or IPCA (other assets). This calculator shows month-by-month evolution with all corrections applied.

q2.question: Which is better: consortium or financing?
q2.answer: It depends on your profile and needs. Consortiums have no interest, but have an administration fee and you may need to wait for contemplation (or pay bid/premium). Financing has interest, but you receive the asset immediately. Use our comparison calculator to see which option leaves more money in your pocket.

q3.question: What is the administration fee in a consortium?
q3.answer: The administration fee is the cost charged by the administrator to manage the consortium group. It's calculated on the total asset value and distributed throughout installments. There are no interest rates as in financing, but this fee represents the service cost. Typical values range between 12% and 20% of the asset value.

q4.question: Bid or premium: which to choose?
q4.answer: Bid is when you pay an extra amount to be contemplated before the lottery, reducing the term. Premium is when you buy an already contemplated letter from another participant, receiving the asset immediately. Bid is better if you can wait a few months; premium is better if you need the asset immediately. Compare the total costs of each option.

q5.question: How does annual correction (INCC/IPCA) work in consortiums?
q5.answer: Consortium installments are corrected annually by inflation indices. For real estate, INCC is used; for other assets, IPCA. The correction is applied every 12 months, increasing the value of future installments. That's why extra amortizations generate savings by avoiding adjustments on larger amounts.

q6.question: Is it worth making extra amortizations in a consortium?
q6.answer: Usually yes, especially if you have money available. Extra amortizations reduce the outstanding balance faster, avoid future corrections on larger amounts, and can reduce the term or installment value. The best scenario depends on the annual correction rate and alternative investment options.

q7.question: Does the simulator include all consortium costs?
q7.answer: Not necessarily. The simulation is educational and focuses on administration fee, annual correction, and amortizations. Costs like insurance, reserve fund, contemplation fees, specific bid rules, and other contract clauses may change actual values. Always consult the contract and administrator for exact values.

q1.question: Which is better: loan or consortium?
q1.answer: It depends on your profile and needs. Loan is better if you need the property immediately and can get a good interest rate. Consortium is better if you can wait for contemplation and the admin fee is lower than loan interest. Use this calculator to compare specific scenarios.

q2.question: How does investing the difference work?
q2.answer: When one option has a lower installment than the other, the monthly difference can be invested. For example, if the loan costs R$ 3,000 and the consortium R$ 2,500, you invest R$ 500/month. By the end, this accumulated investment reduces the net cost of the more expensive option, making the comparison fairer.

q3.question: What is net cost?
q3.answer: Net cost is total paid minus income (rent) and minus accumulated investment balance. It's the most important metric to compare both options, as it considers all cash flows: payments, income, and investments.

q4.question: Why is rent considered in the comparison?
q4.answer: If you plan to rent the property, rent income reduces the net cost of both options. In a loan, you receive rent from month 1. In a consortium, you only receive after contemplation (when you have the property). This significantly impacts the comparison.

q5.question: How to interpret IRR in the comparison?
q5.answer: IRR (Internal Rate of Return) shows the financial return of each option considering the future property value. A higher IRR indicates better return. Compare loan and consortium IRRs to see which generates better return on investment.

q6.question: What to do if the result shows a technical tie?
q6.answer: If net cost is practically equal, consider other factors: time need (loan is immediate, consortium needs waiting), flexibility (loan allows extra amortizations), and personal preference. The difference may be so small that other factors become decisive.

q7.question: Does the calculator consider all costs?
q7.answer: The calculator considers main costs: interest, admin fee, annual adjustment, and difference investment. It doesn't necessarily include all costs like insurance, contract fees, taxes, and other specific expenses. Use as an estimate and validate with real proposals from banks and administrators.

q5.answer: Yes, very important! IGPM is usually higher than inflation, so rent increases significantly over time. This can make rent exceed loan payment after a few years, requiring extra contributions. The calculator considers this annual adjustment.

q6.question: Should I consider other costs besides payment and rent?
q6.answer: Yes. When buying, you have costs like property tax, insurance, maintenance, and possible renovations. When renting, you have rent and possible moving costs. The calculator focuses on main costs (payment vs rent), but you should consider other costs in your real decision.

q7.question: How to interpret the result when there's a technical tie?
q7.answer: If final net worth is practically equal, consider other factors: mobility needs (renting is more flexible), stability (buying offers more stability), personal preference, and non-financial factors. The difference may be so small that other factors become decisive.

basics.title: What is IRR (Internal Rate of Return)
basics.p1: The Internal Rate of Return (IRR) is a financial metric that represents the discount rate that makes the net present value (NPV) of a series of cash flows equal to zero. In other words, it's the expected rate of return of an investment or project.
basics.p2: IRR is widely used to evaluate investment feasibility, compare different opportunities, and make financial decisions. The higher the IRR, the more attractive the investment.
basics.p3: IRR is especially useful because it considers the time value of money, recognizing that a dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future.

q1.question: What is IRR and what is it used for?
q1.answer: IRR (Internal Rate of Return) is the discount rate that makes the net present value of an investment equal to zero. It's used to evaluate investment profitability, compare different opportunities, and make financial decisions. The higher the IRR, the more attractive the investment.

q2.question: How to interpret a negative IRR?
q2.answer: A negative IRR indicates the investment is not financially viable - future cash flows don't compensate for the initial investment. This means you would lose money with this investment. Consider other alternatives or review projected cash flows.

q3.question: What's the difference between monthly IRR and annual IRR?
q3.answer: Monthly IRR is calculated considering cash flows occur monthly. Annual IRR is the equivalent annual rate, calculated by converting monthly IRR to an annual rate using the formula: (1 + monthly_IRR)¹² - 1. The calculator shows both to facilitate comparisons with other annual market rates.

q4.question: Can I use negative and positive values in cash flows?
q4.answer: Yes! Negative values represent money outflows (investments, expenses) and positive values represent inflows (revenue, returns). It's essential to have at least one negative flow (initial investment) and at least one positive flow (return) to calculate IRR.

q5.question: How to paste cash flows from a spreadsheet?
q5.answer: You can copy a column or row of values from a spreadsheet (Excel, Google Sheets) and paste directly into the cash flow field. The calculator automatically detects values separated by line breaks or tabs and imports them. Use negative values for outflows and positive values for inflows.

q6.question: Does IRR consider inflation?
q6.answer: Not directly. The calculated IRR uses the nominal values of the entered cash flows. If you want an analysis considering inflation, you should use cash flows already adjusted for expected inflation (real values). The resulting IRR will be a real rate, not nominal.

q7.question: When to use IRR vs other metrics like NPV or payback?
q7.answer: IRR is useful for comparing investments of different sizes and terms, as it shows the percentage return rate. NPV shows the absolute value in currency. Payback shows how long it takes to recover the investment. Use IRR to compare opportunities, NPV to see total value generated, and payback to evaluate liquidity.

whatAre.title: What are compound interest?
whatAre.p1: Compound interest is interest calculated on the initial amount plus accumulated interest from previous periods. Unlike simple interest, where interest is calculated only on the initial amount, compound interest makes money grow exponentially over time.
whatAre.p2: It's the concept behind 'interest on interest' and is considered one of the most powerful forces in the financial universe. The longer you leave money invested, the greater the effect of compound interest.
whatAre.p3: Compound interest is widely used in investments such as savings accounts, CDB, Treasury bonds, stocks, and other financial products that yield over time.

compound.title: Compound Interest
compound.explanation: Interest is calculated on the initial capital plus accumulated interest. Growth is exponential and much faster over time. Used in most investments.

q1.question: What's the difference between simple and compound interest?
q1.answer: Simple interest is calculated only on the initial capital, resulting in linear growth. Compound interest is calculated on the initial capital plus accumulated interest, resulting in exponential growth. For long-term investments, compound interest generates much more return.

q2.question: How to convert annual rate to monthly?
q2.answer: To convert annual rate to monthly, use the formula: monthly rate = (1 + annual rate)^(1/12) - 1. For example, 12% per year ≈ 0.95% per month. The calculator allows choosing between monthly or annual period, so you just need to enter the rate corresponding to the selected period.

q3.question: Do periodic contributions also earn compound interest?
q3.answer: Yes! Each periodic contribution also earns compound interest from the period it's made. For example, a contribution made in month 5 earns compound interest for the remaining months. This significantly accelerates investment growth.

q4.question: What is the Rule of 72?
q4.answer: The Rule of 72 is a quick way to estimate how long it takes to double an investment. Divide 72 by the annual interest rate. For example, with 6% per year, it takes approximately 12 years to double (72 ÷ 6 = 12).

q5.question: Does the calculator consider taxes and fees?
q5.answer: Not directly. The calculator shows the gross value of compound interest. For real investments, you should consider taxes (such as income tax on earnings) and administrative fees, which reduce net return. Use results as an estimate and adjust as needed.

q6.question: Can I use the calculator for different types of investments?
q6.answer: Yes! The calculator works for any investment that earns compound interest: savings accounts, CDB, Treasury bonds, stocks (considering reinvested dividends), investment funds, etc. Just use the interest rate corresponding to the investment period.

q7.question: How to interpret the growth chart?
q7.answer: The chart shows two lines: 'Total Value' (total investment growth) and 'Accumulated Contributions' (sum of contributions made). The difference between the two lines represents interest earned. The greater the difference over time, the greater the power of compound interest.

q1.question: How does regressive IR calculation work?
q1.answer: Regressive IR varies by term: up to 180 days (22.5%), up to 360 days (20%), up to 720 days (17.5%), and above 720 days (15%). The tax is calculated on profit after deducting IOF, if applicable.

q2.question: When is IOF applied?
q2.answer: IOF is only applied to redemptions with a term of less than 30 days. The rate decreases progressively from day 1 (96%) to day 29 (3%), being zero from day 30 onwards.

q3.question: What does 'real return' mean?
q3.answer: Real return is the net return discounting expected inflation (IPCA). It shows the real purchasing power of the investment, i.e., how much you actually gained above inflation.

q4.question: How does IPCA+ calculation work?
q4.answer: IPCA+ combines inflation (IPCA) with a real spread. For example, IPCA+5% means you receive IPCA plus 5% per year. The calculation considers both components in daily compounding.

q5.question: Why use calendar days instead of business days?
q5.answer: We use calendar days and base 365 to simplify comparison. Although some investments use different conventions (such as 252 business days), our approach allows a consistent comparison between all options.
